messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       2.04    2.09    83.1   0.518      6.14  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL    
S4       1.79    1.82    57.1   0.759      3.21  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Input: Piezo (Ip, f, Cp). $V_{oc}$ is around 3.2V (S1).
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled mean)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (absolute max)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (startup time)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (stability)
    *   Operating Conditions (S1-S6): Varying $I_p, f, C_p, R_L$, and Temperature.
    *   Piezo Model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and 20M$\Omega$ resistance.

    *   S1: nominal.
    *   S2: low f (50Hz), mid load (680k).
    *   S3: high f (200Hz), small $C_p$ (17.5nF), light load (4.7M). $V_{oc}$ will be higher.
    *   S4: low f (50Hz), large $C_p$ (32.5nF), mid load (1M).
    *   S5: high f (200Hz), large $C_p$ (32.5nF), heavy load (150k).
    *   S6: hot (85C), heavy load (200k).

    *   Reference design FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) fails on:
        *   S2: ripple, startup, settled.
        *   S3: $v_{max}$ (it exceeds 3.6V).
        *   S4: $v_{avg}$, ripple, startup, settled.
        *   S5: $v_{avg}$, startup.
        *   S6: $v_{avg}$, startup.
    *   Observations:
        *   FBR doesn't provide enough voltage for heavy loads (S5, S6) or low frequency (S2, S4).
        *   FBR exceeds 3.6V for light loads (S3).
        *   FBR is passive and depends on $C_p$ discharging through the diodes.

    *   The piezo energy harvester typically uses SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) or a buck/boost converter.
    *   Since we have a `SYNC` controller and an inductor `L`, we can implement an SSHI-like flip or a switched-capacitor-like stage.
    *   The goal is to maximize the charge extracted from $C_p$.
    *   A simple SSHI circuit uses an inductor to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the voltage seen by the rectifier.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI (Parallel-SSHI / SECE style)**
        *   We need a rectifier (Full Bridge) to get energy into the storage capacitor `out`.
        *   We need a switching mechanism to invert the voltage on $C_p$.
        *   Structure: Piezo terminals (pzp, pzn). Full bridge (D1-D4) to `out`. A switch (S1) and inductor (L1) in parallel with the piezo (or some variation).
        *   Actually, a simpler approach for the "flipped" voltage is a "synchronous rectifier" or a "buck-boost" topology, but we are limited by the `SYNC` component's behavior (fixed `ton` at extrema).
        *   A classic SSHI: The inductor $L$ is connected across the piezo terminals via a switch $S$ that closes at the peaks. This flips $V_{Cp}$.
        *   Wait, the `SYNC` closes for `ton`. If $L$ is in parallel with $C_p$ (via $S$), the energy oscillates. $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC_p}$. To flip the voltage, we need $t_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$.

    *   **Design 2: Zener Clamping**
        *   S3 failed due to $v_{max} > 3.6\text{ V}$. A Zener diode `DZ33` on the output node `out` will clamp the voltage to 3.3V, satisfying $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$.

    *   **Design 3: Boost/Charge Pump variant?**
        *   The `SYNC` controller allows us to create a switched-inductor circuit.
        *   Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" or an SSHI-enhanced bridge.

    *   **Proposed Design A: SSHI-enhanced FBR**
        *   Components:
            *   Full bridge (DSCH) from piezo (pzp, pzn) to `out`.
            *   L1 and S1 in parallel with the piezo (pzp to pzn).
            *   S1 controlled by G1 (SYNC, edges="both", phase=0).
            *   C_out on `out` to 0.
            *   D_zener (DZ33) from `out` to 0 to protect against overvoltage (S3).

    *   **Proposed Design B: Buck-Boost-like structure (using SYNC)**
        *   If we put L1 in series with the piezo and a switch to ground, we can build a boost converter. But `SYNC` is geared towards peaks.
        *   Let's stick to SSHI concepts.

    *   **Proposed Design C: Half-Bridge/Simplified Rectifier with Zener**
        *   Maybe just a bridge with a better $C_{out}$ and a Zener for S3? But the FBR failed heavily on S5 and S6 (heavy load), meaning it's not extracting enough energy. SSHI is necessary.

    *   Piezo: pzp, pzn.
    *   Bridge:
        *   D1: pzp -> out
        *   D2: pzn -> out
        *   D3: 0 -> pzp
        *   D4: 0 -> pzn
    *   SSHI:
        *   L1: pzp -> n1
        *   S1: n1 -> pzn (controlled by G1)
        *   G1: SYNC, edges="both", ton=... (to be optimized), phase=0.
    *   Storage:
        *   C1: out -> 0.
    *   Protection:
        *   D5: 0 -> out (DZ33) - *Wait, check Zener orientation*: "zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out)".

    *   *Refining the SSHI*: In a basic SSHI, the inductor flips the voltage on $C_p$. The rectifier then takes the rectified peaks. This significantly increases the average current into the storage capacitor.

    *   *Verification of component count*: 4 diodes (bridge) + 1 zener + 1 inductor + 1 switch + 1 SYNC + 1 capacitor = 8 components. Well within the 16 limit.

    *   L1 value: $C_p$ is ~25nF. For $t_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$, if $L=10\text{mH}$, $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-2} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.14 \times \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \times 1.58 \times 10^{-5} \approx 50\text{ }\mu\text{s}$. This fits the `ton` range (1e-7 to 1e-3).

    *   What if the bridge is too lossy? DSCH is 0.25V. Two diodes in series = 0.5V.
    *   What if $V_{out}$ needs to be higher? The SSHI helps by increasing the voltage peaks.

    *   *Alternative Topology (Non-inverting boost?)*:
        *   Maybe a simpler approach for some cases is a charge pump, but we have an inductor.

    *   *Wait, check the SYNC phase*:
        *   Piezo current $I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
        *   Voltage $V_p$ peaks when $I_p$ is 0 (zero crossings).
        *   `SYNC` closes at "piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current". This is exactly what we need for SSHI.

    *   *Topology 1 (SSHI-FBR)*:
        - Bridge (D1-D4)
        - Zener (D5)
        - L1 + S1 in parallel with piezo
        - C1 on out
        - SYNC G1

    *   *Topology 2 (Simplified SSHI / SECE style)*:
        - Maybe a different way to connect the inductor.
        - In some SECE designs, the inductor is not just in parallel but used to transfer charge.
        - However, the "flipped" $C_p$ voltage is the most robust basic SSHI.

    *   *Topology 3 (Half-bridge SSHI)*:
        - Using a half-bridge rectifier if pzn is grounded. But pzn is not grounded.

    *   *Wait, let's consider the a "Synchronous" switch as the rectifier itself?*
        - We have only 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.
        - Using SYNC as a rectifier:
            S1: pzp -> out, G1 (edges="pos")
            S2: pzn -> out, G1 (edges="neg")
            S3: out -> pzp, G2... (No, that's complex).
        - Stick to the diode bridge; it's reliable.

    - Topology 1: Full bridge + Zener + SSHI (Parallel L-S).
    - Topology 2: Full bridge + Zener + an L-C-S combination for better energy transfer (though L-S is standard). Let's try a slightly different L-S placement or just a variant with a larger capacitor.
    - Actually, let's try:
        1. SSHI-FBR (Inductor flips $C_p$ voltage).
        2. FBR with Zener but no SSHI (to see if Zener alone fixes S3 and the optimizer finds a better $C_{out}$ for the others, though unlikely).
        3. A Buck-Boost approach: L1 from pzp to n1, S1 from n1 to 0. This is a boost. G1 edges="both". D1 from n1 to out. This would be a very different power stage.

    - Let's refine Topology 3 (Boost):
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S1: n1 -> 0 (G1, edges="both")
        D1: n1 -> out
        This collects energy when S1 is open. But pzp is AC. This might not work.

    - Let's stick to the most promising: SSHI-FBR.
    - For a second option, let's try a "half-bridge" if it's possible, but the piezo model is floating.
    - Let's try an SSHI with the inductor in a different position? No, parallel is the way.
    - Let's try a design with only 2 diodes (half-bridge) and a large capacitor, though that usually requires a grounded terminal.

    - Wait, looking at the components again: `S` is a switch, `SYNC` is the controller.
    - Let's propose:
        1. SSHI + FBR + Zener. (Most robust)
        2. SSHI + FBR (No Zener, let the optimizer try to handle $v_{max}$ via $L$ and $C$).
        3. FBR + Zener (No SSHI, just to check).

    - Actually, let's try a "Voltage Doubler" style if possible? No, the inductor is key.

    - Let's refine the SSHI-FBR again.
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1)
        C1: out -> 0
        G1: edges="both", ton=... phase=0.

    - Is there any other way to use the SYNC?
        Maybe a "Synchronous Rectifier"?
        S1: pzp -> out (G1, pos)
        S2: pzn -> out (G1, neg)
        S3: 0 -> pzp (G2, neg)
        S4: 0 -> pzn (G2, pos)
        This replaces the diode bridge with switches. Ron=2 Ohm is much lower than the diode drop. This would help significantly with S5 and S6 (heavy load).

    - Let's try this "Synchronous Bridge" + Zener:
        S1: pzp -> out, G1, edges="pos"
        S2: pzn -> out, G1, edges="neg"
        S3: 0 -> pzp, G2, edges="neg"
        S4: 0 -> pzn, G2, edges="pos"
        C1: out -> 0
        D1: 0 -> out (DZ33)
        G1: phase=0, ton=...
        G2: phase=0, ton=...

    - But wait, the SYNC controller closes for `ton` at the extrema.
        At the positive peak of $V_{pzp}$, $V_{pzp}$ is max. We want S1 (pzp->out) and S4 (0->pzn) to be closed.
        At the negative peak of $V_{pzp}$, $V_{pzn}$ is max. We want S2 (pzn->out) and S3 (0->pzp) to be closed.
        So:
        G1: edges="pos" (closes at max $V_{pzp}$), controls S1 and S4.
        G2: edges="neg" (closes at min $V_{pzp}$), controls S2 and S3.
        Wait, the prompt says "at most 4 switches".
        S1: pzp -> out, ctrl: G1
        S4: 0 -> pzn, ctrl: G1
        S2: pzn -> out, ctrl: G2
        S3: 0 -> pzp, ctrl: G2
        This is a synchronous bridge.

    - Now, can we combine Synchronous Bridge + SSHI?
        That would require more than 4 switches. (Bridge=4, SSHI=1).
        We only have 4 switches.
        So we can have either a synchronous bridge OR a diode bridge + SSHI.

    - Let's compare:
        - SSHI + Diode Bridge: Increases $V_{in}$ to the bridge.
        - Synchronous Bridge: Reduces the $V_{drop}$ of the bridge.
        Given $V_{oc}$ is ~3.2V and $V_{out}$ target is 1.8V, the 0.5V drop of DSCH is significant but not devastating. The main issue is the energy extraction efficiency. SSHI is generally more powerful for piezo.

    - Let's provide:
        1. SSHI + Diode Bridge + Zener.
        2. Synchronous Bridge + Zener.
        3. SSHI + Diode Bridge (No Zener).

    *Wait*, the Synchronous Bridge alone doesn't "flip" the voltage to increase extraction; it just reduces losses. SSHI is better for the "heavy load" failures (S5, S6) because it extracts more energy per cycle.

    Let's stick to SSHI + Diode Bridge as the primary.

    *Final check on SSHI design*:
    L1: pzp -> n1
    S1: n1 -> pzn
    G1: edges="both", phase=0, ton=...
    Wait, if $S1$ is in parallel with the piezo, does it need a diode to prevent the storage cap from discharging back into the inductor? No, the bridge diodes prevent that.

    *   D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
    *   D2: pzn, out (DSCH)
    *   D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
    *   D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
    *   D5: 0, out (DZ33)
    *   L1: pzp, n1
    *   S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
    *   G1: SYNC (edges="both", phase=0)
    *   C1: out, 0

    *   D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
    *   D2: pzn, out (DSCH)
    *   D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
    *   D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
    *   C1: out, 0
    *   L1: pzp, n1
    *   S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
    *   G1: SYNC (edges="both", phase=0)

    *   S1: pzp, out (ctrl: G1)
    *   S2: pzn, out (ctrl: G2)
    *   S3: 0, pzp (ctrl: G2)
    *   S4: 0, pzn (ctrl: G1)
    *   G1: SYNC (edges="pos", phase=0)
    *   G2: SYNC (edges="neg", phase=0)
    *   D1: 0, out (DZ33)
    *   C1: out, 0

    Wait, in Topology 3, does the SYNC close at the correct time?
    "closes its switches ... at the piezo voltage extrema".
    At positive peak (extrema), $V_{pzp}$ is max, $V_{pzn}$ is min.
    G1 (edges="pos") closes S1 (pzp->out) and S4 (0->pzn). Perfect.
    At negative peak (extrema), $V_{pzp}$ is min, $V_{pzn}$ is max.
    G2 (edges="neg") closes S2 (pzn->out) and S3 (0->pzp). Perfect.

    *Self-Correction*: For the SSHI, the inductor value and `ton` are critical. The evolution strategy will optimize them, but I'll provide reasonable starting values.
    $L=10\text{mH}$, $t_{on}=50\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.

    Wait, a detail: `S` components have `Ron = 2 Ohm`. In the synchronous bridge, the total resistance is $2 \times 2\text{ }\Omega = 4\text{ }\Omega$. In the diode bridge, the drop is $\sim 0.5\text{V}$. At $50\text{ }\mu\text{A}$, $0.5\text{V}$ is much more significant than $4\text{ }\Omega \times 50\text{ }\mu\text{A} = 200\text{ }\mu\text{V}$. So the synchronous bridge is indeed more efficient.

    However, the SSHI is the only way to really beat the $V_{oc}$ limit. Let's see.

    One more look at the `SYNC` phase. `phase` shifts the pulses. For SSHI, $t_{on}$ usually starts exactly at the peak. So `phase=0` is correct.

    - SSHI-FBR-Zener (Best chance for overall)
    - Sync-Bridge-Zener (Best efficiency, but no voltage boost)
    - SSHI-FBR (No zener, just for comparison)

    Actually, let's replace "SSHI-FBR (no zener)" with "Synchronous-Bridge-SSHI" if possible?
    Wait, Sync-Bridge uses 4 switches. SSHI uses 1 switch. Total = 5 switches. Max is 4.
    Can't do both.

    Let's try "Half-Bridge SSHI" as the 3rd option?
    If we ground pzn:
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: 0 -> pzp (Wait, this is not a bridge)
    No, the floating piezo is the standard model.

    Let's go with:
    1. SSHI-FBR-Zener
    2. Sync-Bridge-Zener
    3. SSHI-FBR (no zener) - Actually, let's try SSHI with only a half-bridge (2 diodes) and see if it's more efficient.
    L1: pzp, n1
    S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
    D1: pzp, out
    D2: pzn, out (No, that doesn't work)

    Let's just use these three:
    1. `sshi_fbr_zener`
    2. `sync_bridge_zener`
    3. `sshi_fbr`

    Wait, I just noticed something. The reference design FBR used 2.2uF. For ripple $\le 0.05\text{V}$ at $R_L=150\text{k}\Omega$ (S5), we might need a larger capacitor or a better rectifier. $2.2\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ might be too small. The optimizer will handle it.

    *Double check the Zener* again: "zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out)".
    My D5: ["0", "out"]. Correct.
